CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: China should announce retaliatory tariffs on the remaining ~$60 billion of US goods not yet covered, matching the US escalation on $200 billion (raised from 10% to 25%) and the threatened expansion to an additional $300 billion. Retaliation signals resolve, preserves negotiating leverage, and deters further US escalation by raising costs on both sides. China should simultaneously leave the door open for resumed negotiations, framing retaliation as defensive and WTO-consistent.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat score of +0.55 reflects a high and escalating threat to China's export economy. The US has already imposed tariffs on $250 billion of Chinese goods and on May 10, 2019 raised tariffs on $200 billion from 10% to 25%, with Trump calling for tariffs on 'essentially all remaining imports from China, which are valued at approximately $300 billion' (Fox Business, May 2019). This threatens to cover nearly all Chinese exports to the US (~$500 billion+), which would severely disrupt China's export hubs and manufacturing employment. The BBC notes the yuan fell over 5% against the dollar in 2018, and the Shanghai Composite slumped nearly 25%, indicating financial market stress. The USC analysis warns that the dispute is fundamentally about 'the most important and potentially profitable industries of the future — AI, cloud computing, robotics, green tech,' meaning the stakes go beyond trade balances to China's industrial upgrading goals (Made in China 2025). Senator Graham explicitly stated the US strategy is 'to break the stranglehold China has on the supply chain' (Fox Business). This is an existential-level strategic threat dressed as a trade dispute.

The action score of -1 (maximal retaliation, within the retaliate band) is justified because: (1) China has already retaliated on $110 billion of US goods and announced new levies on $60 billion in response to the May escalation (USC/Annenberg), so this is a continuation of established doctrine; (2) Retaliation preserves bargaining leverage — conceding now without a deal framework would invite further demands; (3) China can target politically sensitive US goods (soybeans, chemicals, whiskey in Republican districts, per BBC) to raise domestic US political costs; (4) The US side has acknowledged 'both sides will suffer' (Kudlow, Fox Business), meaning retaliation has real bite. However, China should avoid matching the full $300 billion threat tit-for-tat immediately, as its import base from the US (~$120 billion) is smaller, and instead signal willingness to negotiate if the US de-escalates.
key_factors: US raised tariffs on $200bn of Chinese goods from 10% to 25% on May 10, 2019
Trump threatened tariffs on remaining ~$300bn of Chinese imports
China already retaliated on $110bn of US goods and announced levies on $60bn more
Dispute is fundamentally about tech competition (AI, cloud, robotics) not just trade balances
Yuan depreciated 5% vs USD in 2018; Shanghai Composite fell 25%
US strategy explicitly aims to break China's supply chain dominance
IMF cut 2019 global growth forecast citing US-China tensions
China's retaliatory tariffs strategically target goods from Republican districts

sources_cited.excerpt: Chinese officials responded to President Donald Trump's decision to raise tariffs on $200 billion in Chinese imports with an announcement Monday that China will impose its own new levies on $60 billion of American products. The negotiations are not principally about current buying and selling, but rather about the most important and potentially profitable industries of the future. These include artificial intelligence, cloud computing, robotics and green tech.
